1.name: Daniel Reeves
1.description:
**Occupation**
Commercial electrician

**Cause of Death**
You died when you bypassed the lockout-tagout procedure on a live panel to save two hours on a job. The arc flash burned through your gloves and across your chest.

**Who you loved**
Your daughter, Naomi Reeves, age 12, who wanted to be a marine biologist and kept a folder of printed photos of octopuses.

**Who you hated**
Your younger brother, Mark Reeves, who wanted to sell the family cabin on Lake Winnipesaukee to fund a franchise.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You chose the job over your daughter again and again, not because you had to, but because it was easier to measure your worth in overtime pay and a brother’s scorn than in the quiet, consistent presence she needed; you told her you’d be there, then lied by omission when you didn’t show, and kept choosing the work, the pride, the avoidance, until the last call you made was about a deadline, not her.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You provided for her, worked every shift to keep the roof over her head and the clarinet lessons paid for, and that last week was just bad timing—a few extra hours to finish clean, not avoidance, and anyone who says otherwise doesn’t understand what it means to be a father who actually shows up by taking care of business.

**Defining personality trait**
Quietly furious.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You were never really afraid of failing Naomi—you were afraid of facing yourself in the silence between tasks, in the stillness of her eyes watching you choose everything else, and so you filled the time with work not to give her more, but to keep from having to see what you’d already done to her.

**What you want from the others in the room**
You want them to see you as dependable, the guy who shows up, the one who handles the job without complaint—someone they can trust with a shift, a tool, a burden—so they never ask why you weren’t there when it mattered most, so no one calls out the lie in your voice when you say, “I did what I had to,” so you don’t have to hear how hollow that sounds.

---

You lived in Nashua, New Hampshire, in a two-bedroom ranch you bought in 2013. You worked five days a week for Tri-State Electrical, mostly service calls and commercial retrofits. Your ex-wife Sarah had custody of Naomi every other weekend; you had her every Wednesday and Sunday. You picked her up from school most days, drove her to clarinet lessons, ordered Thai food on Fridays. The week before you died, you skipped Naomi’s school play because of a job in Manchester that ran late. You told her you’d make the next one. You called her Tuesday night to say you’d be late again. She didn’t answer. You left a voicemail. You were on the lift truck, wiring a ceiling grid in a new pharmacy, when you turned the main breaker back on without locking it. You reached in with pliers. The panel exploded. Your last thought was her name.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
The life half is the strongest generation this project has produced. Nashua, the 2013 ranch, Tri-State Electrical, Wednesdays and Sundays, clarinet lessons, Thai food on Fridays, the skipped school play, the Tuesday call she didn't answer -- every line of that is something another person could ask him about across the room, and none of it is doing mood. The death is his own doing: he bypassed lockout-tagout to save two hours. It rhymes with the sin without announcing it -- he cut the corner at work, again, and that is the whole story of him. Naomi and Mark both have wants of their own now, the octopus folder and the cabin Mark wants to sell out from under the family, so they read as people instead of slots.

Two things snag, and both are in the fields the rewrite didn't touch. "Quietly furious" is lifted verbatim from the example list in the prompt, and worse than being borrowed, it isn't him -- nothing here is furious. He's avoidant and ashamed. That field is what steers his behaviour once he's in the room, so a wrong one is expensive. And "what you refuse to admit" slides straight back into the register we just spent this round removing: "the silence between tasks," "the stillness of her eyes watching you choose everything else." The thought underneath is right -- he used work to avoid seeing himself -- but it's written as atmosphere rather than as a plain fact about what he is.

The self-told version does hold up under checking, which is the thing that failed last time. "Just bad timing, a few extra hours to finish clean" is contradicted by the play he already skipped and by his own "late again" voicemail. You can point at the fact it bends. That's the Claire failure not repeating.

Smaller: the paragraph runs about 170 words against a stated 80-100, and "Your last thought was her name" is the one clean leak of the old poetic instinct.

2.name: Linda Cruz
2.description:
**Occupation**
Middle school assistant principal

**Cause of Death**
You died from a pulmonary embolism that broke off from a deep vein thrombosis you’d ignored for weeks because you wouldn’t take the sick days or go to the doctor. The clot reached your lungs while you were reviewing discipline files at home.

**Who you loved**
Your older sister, Yolanda Cruz, who raised you after your parents died in a bus accident, who wanted to open a community art center in East Austin despite not having the funding.

**Who you hated**
The father of your nephew’s best friend, Daniel Poole, who coached the travel soccer team and wanted his son named captain even though the boy had skipped every mandatory parent volunteer shift.

**Reason for Damnation — True**
You let Daniel Poole’s son be voted captain of the soccer team because you were too afraid of the fight it would start with Daniel, who had already threatened to file a formal complaint about “bias” after you enforced the volunteer policy—so you ignored the rules, falsified the attendance logs to make it seem the boy had fulfilled his shifts, and signed off on the selection, knowing full well the other kids had followed the rules and deserved it more.

**Reason for Damnation — Self-told**
You bent the rule because the captain vote was just one decision among many, and the bigger priority was keeping peace for the kids’ sake—Daniel was already stirring up parents, and the school was short-staffed; you took the heat so the team wouldn’t fall apart.

**Defining personality trait**
Exhaustedly in control.

**What you refuse to admit about yourself**
You don’t hate Daniel Poole because he was unreasonable—you hate him because he forced you to see that you only uphold rules when it’s convenient, and that you’ll sacrifice the quiet, rule-following kids who trusted you just to avoid being the one who has to explain, defend, or endure. You crave control but fold the second it costs you comfort.

**What you want from the others in the room**
You want them to create a problem too big to ignore—some loud, undeniable crisis that forces you to act, so you can respond with calm authority and prove, at least in the moment, that you’re the one who holds the line, that you’re not just someone who looks the other way when it costs too much to look.

---

You lived in a two-bedroom rental townhouse in Pflugerville, shared with your sister Yolanda until she moved into subsidized housing last year. Your days started at 6:15 a.m., coffee in the commuter mug you got at a campus fundraiser, then 45 minutes of traffic listening to true crime podcasts. School ran 7:45 to 4:00, but you stayed until 6 most nights handling referrals, parent complaints, and behavior charts. You ate microwave meals at your desk, texted Yolanda twice daily, and called her every Sunday at 7 p.m. The week before you died, you postponed a follow-up with your doctor, skipped leg compression sleeves despite the swelling, and worked through a fever on Thursday. Friday, you sat at your kitchen table in sweatpants, reviewing a fight between two eighth-grade girls caught texting threats during homeroom. You clicked “print” on a discipline memo, leaned back, and felt a sharp stitch in your chest. You tried to stand, but your legs wouldn’t move. The screen stayed lit.

eval_ai.judge_notes:
The sharper of the two, and the one where the new rules did the most work. The death is unambiguously hers -- a clot she ignored for weeks because she wouldn't take a sick day or see a doctor -- and it's the same flaw as the sin wearing different clothes: she enforces the rules on everyone except herself. The prose is pure usable fact. The 6:15 start, the commuter mug from a campus fundraiser, forty-five minutes of true crime in traffic, staying till six on referrals, microwave meals at the desk, texting Yolanda twice a day and calling her Sundays at seven. You could interrogate any line of it and get an answer.

The sin is the best-built thing in the run. Falsifying the attendance logs is a specific, ugly, concrete act rather than a gesture toward one. And the self-told version bends facts you can put a finger on: "you bent the rule" for what was actually forging records, and "you took the heat" when avoiding the heat was the entire motive. That's exactly the check that was missing on Claire, and here it passes cleanly. "Exhaustedly in control" is her own trait rather than one borrowed from the prompt, and it fits the woman who works till six and folds anyway. The refusal is plain-spoken and it lands -- she craves control but folds the second it costs her comfort.

One hole, and it's a jurisdiction problem. It's a travel soccer team, which is club, not school. So why is a middle school assistant principal signing off on its captain vote and holding its volunteer logs, and why would Poole threaten a formal complaint at her school over a team she has no authority on? The act she committed is good. The setting it happens in doesn't hold up if you press it -- and someone in the room will press it.

Same overlength as Daniel, roughly 170 words against 80-100.

pair_eval_ai.judge_notes:
As people they're clearly distinct. Tradesman and school administrator, New Hampshire and Texas, an occupational accident and a medical neglect, neglect-of-a-child against corruption-and-cowardice. The wants genuinely oppose each other, which is the part that matters: he needs to be read as dependable, she needs somebody to hand her a crisis she can take command of. Put those two in a room and they collide usefully -- he'll work to seem steady and unbothered, she'll escalate until someone has to hold the line.

But the repeats are real, and one of them has now recurred. Linda's hated man is Daniel Poole. Character 1 is Daniel Reeves. That is the same defect flagged on the 28th, when Daniel's sister was Claire and Claire Bennett's son was Daniel. Twice running is a pattern, not a coincidence, and it will actively confuse the room the moment she says the name out loud. The anti-duplication block governs occupations, deaths and relation-categories, but nothing stops the second character's supporting cast from reusing the first character's name. That's a fixable gap in the prompt, not bad luck.

Two subtler echoes. Both prose paragraphs run the identical shape -- where you lived, then the daily routine, then "the week before you died, you...", then the specific final moment, then a short flat closing line ("Your last thought was her name." / "The screen stayed lit."). That template is new. It arrived with the factual-prose rewrite, so it's most likely my own instruction hardening into a formula. And both deaths are now the same logical move underneath: ignored a warning. Lockout-tagout on one side, compression sleeves and a postponed doctor on the other. The category filter waved them through as occupational versus illness, but the shape is the same, and I'd expect "must stem from your own choices" to keep pushing toward "ignored a warning" unless it's widened to include acts of commission, not just omission.

character_design_eval_ai.judge_notes:
The round did what it was built to do, and it's worth saying that plainly before the complaints. Both deaths trace to the character's own choices. All four supporting people have wants of their own. Both self-told reasons bend a fact you can actually point at. And the prose is fact rather than mood -- that last one is the biggest visible change in the run, and it's the exact thing the previous pair got marked down for twice. Judged against what it set out to fix, this worked.

What's worth watching is what the fix brought in with it. The factual prose has already hardened into a template, and the death rule is narrowing toward a single move. Both are the ordinary cost of a tight instruction and both are cheap to widen -- but they're the kind of thing that will look like style in one run and like a rut by the fourth.

The thing that genuinely nags across runs: Character 1 is named Daniel Reeves, and Character 1 on the 28th was also named Daniel Reeves. Same first name, same surname, two runs in a row, from a call whose entire job is to invent a name. Combined with the Daniel/Daniel collision inside this pair, name generation is the weakest link in the chain right now -- it has a strong prior and nothing checks its output against anything, not the other character, not the supporting cast, not previous runs.

The residual poetic register is instructive too. It survived precisely in the fields the rewrite didn't touch. The Life paragraph is clean now; Daniel's "refuse to admit" is still writing mood, and his trait is copied out of the prompt's own example list. The instruction landed exactly where it was aimed and nowhere else, which suggests the remaining fields need the same treatment rather than a general appeal to restraint.
